keys.text: DNA is not built to last forever.
Its strands break.

keys.text: Hares.

Evidence of a mastodon lineage.
And around those animal traces, plants: poplar, birch, conifers, shrubs and herbs.

keys.text: And DNA did not discover that greener past alone.
Pollen and visible plant remains had already provided clues.
The genetic evidence added another route, especially into animal life with scarce fossil traces.
Suddenly, the mastodon was no longer a strange detail floating in an empty landscape.

keys.text: For a moment, imagine it.
An elephant-like animal moving past trees.
A goose lifting from the water.
Plants where today's landscape looks almost empty.
That is our reconstruction, not a recovered afternoon.
The fragments do not tell us that this animal passed that tree while that bird took flight.
Remember the delivery system: water moves material, and deposits gather it over time.
Nor do these traces give us the giant's exact coat, size or behaviour.
The evidence can support a community without supplying every detail of its members.

keys.text: That boundary matters.
Without it, a plausible scene can quietly become a false memory of something scientists actually saw.
Yet drawing the boundary does not erase the world behind it.
It tells us which parts we have evidence for—and which parts we are imagining.
There is a mistake we can make even when we draw nothing extra.
We can assume that whatever is missing from the DNA was missing from the landscape.
But perhaps an organism's material did not survive.
Perhaps it never reached the samples.
Perhaps the surviving pieces could not be recognised.
No signal is not the same as no animal.
That is why different kinds of evidence matter.
In this study, DNA revealed plant groups that were not recorded there through pollen or larger remains.
Different methods leave different gaps.
Put them together, and the picture can grow without pretending it is complete.

sequences.action: one-off narrative progression; no recycled rendered clip

keys.text: We cannot count every life that passed through this place.
We can still discover that the place once held a world very different from the one we see now.
Come back to the dirt.
No tusk curling out of it.
No skeleton waiting underneath.

keys.text: No complete genome from which to rebuild a mastodon.
Just surviving fragments.

keys.text: Yet those fragments helped connect an animal to a vanished community, and an almost empty-looking place to a greener past.

keys.text: The answer was not to squeeze the animal into today's landscape.
It was to discover how different the landscape used to be.
We have not brought that world back.
We have learned to recognise some of what it left behind.
That forest is gone.
Those ancient lives are over.
What looked like empty ground was an incomplete record.
And we had learned to read part of it.
This is Extinct Life.

sentences.text: There is a mistake we can make even when we draw nothing extra.
We can assume that whatever is missing from the DNA was missing from the landscape.
But perhaps an organism's material did not survive.
Perhaps it never reached the samples.
Perhaps the surviving pieces could not be recognised.
No signal is not the same as no animal.
That is why different kinds of evidence matter.
In this study, DNA revealed plant groups that were not recorded there through pollen or larger remains.
Different methods leave different gaps.
Put them together, and the picture can grow without pretending it is complete.
We cannot count every life that passed through this place.
We can still discover that the place once held a world very different from the one we see now.

sentences.text: Come back to the dirt.
No tusk curling out of it.
No skeleton waiting underneath.
No complete genome from which to rebuild a mastodon.
Just surviving fragments.
Yet those fragments helped connect an animal to a vanished community, and an almost empty-looking place to a greener past.
At the beginning, the puzzle was how to fit a mastodon into northern Greenland.
The answer was not to squeeze the animal into today's landscape.
It was to discover how different the landscape used to be.
We have not brought that world back.
We have learned to recognise some of what it left behind.
That forest is gone.
Those ancient lives are over.
What looked like empty ground was an incomplete record.
And we had learned to read part of it.
This is Extinct Life.
